reason: A judges the practice of behavior-preserving refactoring itself, while B judges whether tests are the tool used to shape design and enable that refactoring, so a PR can refactor well via smell-driven judgment without test-driven practice or vice versa.
A judges the substance of failure handling and error context, while B judges only spelling/grammar of error strings, so a PR can handle failures robustly with typo'd messages or vice versa.
Both score the same property: whether the test suite follows a pyramid shape weighted toward fast unit tests with fewer integration and minimal E2E/UI tests.
A judges the scope/size of the change itself, while B judges the formatting of the commit message text, which are independent properties.

A judges CAP-aware consistency trade-off and conflict-resolution decisions, while B judges whether operational mechanisms like redundancy and traffic-shaping actually keep the system running, so a system can make sound trade-offs without robust redundancy or vice versa.

A judges a structural property of the production code (is it decoupled/seamed for testing), while B judges the rigor of the testing process/methodology itself, so code can be well-structured for testing without a disciplined TDD/BDD process or vice versa.
Both ask the identical question: does the PR include automated tests covering the changed behavior.
Both score the same property: whether tests target externally observable, user-facing behavior rather than implementation internals.

A judges general module/class boundary and visibility organization, while B additionally covers idiomatic Rust API ergonomics (constructors, macros, extension traits, feature flags) that is a distinct dimension beyond organization/visibility.
Both score the same property: whether import statements are placed at the top and consistently grouped, ordered, and deduplicated.

A judges overall testing rigor and methodology (coverage, artifacts, discipline), while B judges specifically whether tests are used to actively shape design decisions, so a suite can be rigorous without being design-driving or vice versa.

A judges the enforcement/governance of static analysis (CI gating, not disabling checks, auto-fix), while B judges the quality/actionability of the findings themselves, so enforcement can be strict while findings are noisy or vice versa.

A judges a structural property of the code (testable seams/decoupling), while B judges a practice of actively using tests to drive design decisions, so code can end up testable through good architecture without TDD-style test-driven design.
Both ask the identical question: does the description explain the reason or motivation for the change rather than just describing it.
Both score the same property: sparse, accurate, why-focused comments that avoid restating self-explanatory code.
Both score the same property: whether commit/PR messages clearly convey what and why with sufficient context for reviewers.

A centers on export style (named vs default, type-only exports) while B centers on import style (ESM vs require, relative/absolute path conventions), so a PR can follow one rule set while violating the other.
